words.title: Celerity
words.definition: Swiftness of movement; rapidity of action or motion.
words.etymology: From Latin **celeritas** (swiftness), from *celer* (swift, quick). Entered English in the late 15th century. The adjective form *celeritous* is rare; the more common relative is *accelerate* — both trace to the same root *celer*.
words.example: The board was urged to proceed with **celerity** on the matter rather than letting it drag on.
words.memoryHook: **Celerity** shares its Latin root with **accelerate** — so anything moving with celerity is accelerating. The "celer" in both words is the same *swift*.

words.title: Alician
words.definition: Surreal, whimsical, or illogical.
words.etymology: From **Alice**, heroine of Lewis Carroll's *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland* (1865) and *Through the Looking-Glass* (1871).
words.example: The meeting took an **Alician** turn when the agenda stopped making sense entirely.
words.memoryHook: **Alician** = like falling down the rabbit hole — rules keep shifting.

words.title: Allopatric
words.definition: Existing or occurring in geographically distinct areas.
words.etymology: From **allo-** (other) + Greek *patra* (fatherland); coined in the context of speciation biology.
words.example: **Allopatric** species evolve in isolation, each adapting to its own corner of the map.
words.memoryHook: *Allo-* (other) + *patra* (fatherland) → **allopatric** = dwelling in a different land.
related: Furcate — both terms about natural division and branching

words.title: Avuncular
words.definition: Kind, friendly, and helpful, like an uncle, in a benevolent or indulgent way.
words.etymology: From Latin **avunculus** (maternal uncle), diminutive of *avus* (grandfather).
words.example: The old foreman had an **avuncular** manner, gruff but quick to look out for the new hires.
words.memoryHook: *Avunculus* = maternal uncle → **avuncular** = uncle-like warmth and good humor.

words.title: Bombinate
words.definition: To buzz; to hum.
words.etymology: From Latin **bombinare** / *bombilare* (to buzz), from *bombus* (a humming, buzzing).
words.example: Her head had become a **bombinating** vacuum after hours of close reading.
words.memoryHook: *Bombus* = the Latin for a buzz, and the genus of bumblebees → to **bombinate** is to buzz like a bee.

words.title: Commensurate
words.definition: Corresponding in size or degree; in proportion.
words.etymology: From Late Latin **commensuratus**, from *com-* (with) + *mensura* (measure).
words.example: Your salary should be **commensurate** with the weight of the responsibility you carry.
words.memoryHook: *Com-* (together) + *mensura* (measure) → things **commensurate** are measured on the same scale.

words.title: Cumberworld
words.definition: A useless person.
words.etymology: From **cumber** (to burden, hinder) + *world*. Middle English.
words.example: The old proverb called an idle dependent a **cumberworld** — a burden nobody wanted.
words.memoryHook: **Cumber** (to burden) + **world** → someone who only encumbers the world.

words.title: Desistance
words.definition: The act of ceasing a behavior, particularly one considered harmful or unwanted.
words.etymology: From Old French **desister**, from Latin *desistere* (to leave off), from *de-* + *sistere* (to stand).
words.example: Studies of criminal **desistance** show that stable work often predicts a drop in offending.
words.memoryHook: *De-* (down/away) + *sistere* (to stand) → to stop standing there; **desistance** = the act of stopping.

words.title: Diachronic
words.definition: Relating to changes occurring over time.
words.etymology: From French **diachronique**, from *dia-* (across) + Greek *khronos* (time).
words.example: A **diachronic** study of the language traces how its grammar shifted across centuries.
words.memoryHook: *Dia-* (across) + *chronos* (time) → **diachronic** = across time. The opposite, *synchronic*, is at one point in time.
related: senescent — change over time applied to aging

words.title: Disject
words.definition: To scatter or disperse.
words.etymology: From Latin **disjicere** (to scatter), from *dis-* (apart) + *jacere* (to throw). First documented use: 1581.
words.example: Can a storm ever be calmer than the stillness it **disjects**?
words.memoryHook: *Dis-* (apart) + *jacere* (throw) → **disject** = throw apart, scatter.

words.title: Éclat
words.definition: Enthusiastic approval; a strikingly brilliant display; notable success.
words.etymology: From French **éclat** (splinter, brilliance), from *éclater* (to burst out) — the same root that gave us *slat* and *eclair*. First documented use: 1676.
words.example: The journal published the hoax with great **éclat**, only to retract it in embarrassment.
words.memoryHook: *Éclat* literally "splinters" like light off a jewel — brilliance that shatters attention.

words.title: Empyrean
words.definition: Relating to heaven or the sky; the highest heaven.
words.etymology: From Greek **empyros** (in fire), from *en* (in) + *pyr* (fire). In medieval cosmology the empyrean was the highest heaven of pure fire and light.
words.example: The **empyrean** domain where human will and God's will became as one.
words.memoryHook: *Pyro* = fire in Greek → **empyrean** = "in fire," the blazing highest heaven.

words.title: Frowze
words.definition: To make untidy, tangled, or ruffled; a wig of frizzed hair.
words.etymology: Origin unknown. First documented use: 1563.
words.example: The wind **frowzed** her hair into a halo of tangles before the interview.
words.memoryHook: Sounds like "frowsy" (unkempt) → **frowze** = to make frowsy.

words.title: Furcate
words.definition: To divide into two or more branches; forked.
words.etymology: From Late Latin **furcatus** (forked), from *furca* (fork).
words.example: The river **furcates** around the island before rejoining downstream.
words.memoryHook: A *furca* is a pitchfork → to **furcate** is to split like a fork's tines.
related: Allopatric — both terms for geographic/natural division

words.title: Imbroglio
words.definition: A difficult, confusing, or embarrassing situation; a confused heap or tangle.
words.etymology: From Italian **imbroglio** (confusion), from *imbrogliare* (to tangle), from *in-* + *broglio* (tangle).
words.example: The contract dispute turned into a legal **imbroglio** no one could untangle.
words.memoryHook: Italian for "tangle" — an **imbroglio** is a knot of complications.
related: Welter — another word for a confused mass

words.title: Indefatigable
words.definition: Incapable of being tired out; persistently energetic and tireless.
words.etymology: From Latin **indefatigabilis**, from *in-* (not) + *defatigare* (to tire out).
words.example: She was an **indefatigable** advocate, still making calls at midnight long after others had quit.
words.memoryHook: *In-* (not) + *defatigare* (to tire) → **indefatigable** = cannot be fatigued.

words.title: Indite
words.definition: To compose or write; to put down in writing; to give literary or formal expression to.
words.etymology: From Latin **indictare** (to proclaim), from *indicere* (to proclaim, declare). An etymological cognate of *indict*: both share the Latin root, but *indict* shifted meaning via Anglo-French legal usage to "to formally accuse or charge with a crime," while *indite* kept the original sense of writing and composing.
words.example: The lawyer was asked to **indite** a formal response to the complaint.
words.memoryHook: To **indite** is to "dictate" words onto the page; its twin *indict* splits off into the courtroom (to accuse), while *indite* stays at the writing desk.

words.title: Melpomenish
words.definition: Tragic; related to tragedy.
words.etymology: From **Melpomene**, the Greek muse of tragedy.
words.example: The third act had a **melpomenish** weight that left the audience silent.
words.memoryHook: Melpomene is the **tragedy** muse; her sister Thalia is comedy → **melpomenish** = tragic.
related: Penelopean — another word from Greek mythology

words.title: Mimetic
words.definition: Copying the behavior, appearance, or characteristics of others.
words.etymology: From Greek **mimetikos** (imitation), from *mimesis*, from *mimeisthai* (to imitate). First documented use: 1632.
words.example: Fashion is a **mimetic** loop — designers copy each other and the public copies them.
words.memoryHook: Think *mime* — a performer who copies — plus the -*etic* suffix → **mimetic** = mime-like imitation.
related: zugunruhe — another word about inherited behavior

words.title: Minacious
words.definition: Threatening or menacing.
words.etymology: From Latin **minari** (to threaten), from *minae* (threats) — ultimately from the Indo-European root *men-* (project), also the source of *menace*, *mountain*, *eminent*, *promenade*, *demean*, *amenable*, and *mouth*. First documented use: 1660. A synonym is *minatory*.
words.example: The gathering clouds had a **minacious** look that hurried the farmers inside.
words.memoryHook: *Minae* = threats in Latin → **minacious** = threat-heavy. Same root as *menace* and *mountain*.
related: Timorous — the fearful response to a threat

words.title: Multifarious
words.definition: Many and of various types; having many varied parts or aspects.
words.etymology: From Latin **multifarius** (manyfold), from *multus* (many) + *-farius*.
words.example: The committee's **multifarious** activities made a single report impossible to write.
words.memoryHook: *Multi-* (many) + *farious* (fold) → **multifarious** = many-fold, many kinds.

words.title: Nefandous
words.definition: So wicked as to defy description; abominable, appalling.
words.etymology: From Latin **nefandus** (wicked), from *ne-* (not) + *fandus* (to be spoken), the gerundive of *fari* (to speak). First documented use: 1649.
words.example: The historian called the massacre **nefandous** — a crime too foul for words.
words.memoryHook: *Ne-* (not) + *fandus* (to be spoken) → **nefandous** = not to be spoken of, unutterably evil.
related: Perfidious — another word for moral evil

words.title: Penelopean
words.definition: Involving repetitive or cyclical efforts, often with little apparent progress; steadfast loyalty and resilience.
words.etymology: From **Penelope**, Odysseus's wife, who held off suitors by weaving a shroud each day and secretly unraveling it each night.
words.example: Rehab felt **Penelopean** — every gain seemed undone by morning, yet she kept at it.
words.memoryHook: Penelope **weaves by day and unravels by night** → work that resets, plus the loyalty to keep going.
related: melpomenish — another word from Greek mythology

words.title: Perfidious
words.definition: Treacherous; deceitful; betraying trust.
words.etymology: From Latin **perfidus** (treacherous), from *per-* (beyond) + *fidus* (faith). First documented use: 1538.
words.example: A **perfidious** ally smiled to your face and sold your plans by night.
words.memoryHook: *Per-* (through/beyond) + *fides* (faith) → one who has gone **past** faith is **perfidious**.
related: nefandous — another word for moral evil

words.title: Pluvial
words.definition: Relating to or characterized by rainfall.
words.etymology: From Latin **pluvialis**, from *pluvia* (rain).
words.example: The alternation of **pluvial** and arid periods shaped the region's ancient climate.
words.memoryHook: *Pluvia* is Latin for rain → **pluvial** = rainy. Picture "pluie," French for rain.

words.title: Propinquity
words.definition: The state of being close to someone or something; proximity; close kinship.
words.etymology: From Latin **propinquitas**, from *propinquus* (near), from *prope* (near).
words.example: He kept his distance, as though afraid **propinquity** might lead him into temptation.
words.memoryHook: *Prope* = near in Latin → **propinquity** = nearness. "Propinquity breeds affection."

words.title: Senescent
words.definition: Growing old; aging; deteriorating with the passage of time.
words.etymology: From Latin **senescere** (to grow old), from *senex* (old).
words.example: The once-vibrant orchard had gone **senescent**, its branches brittle and half bare.
words.memoryHook: *Senex* = old man in Latin → **senescent** = aging. The prefix *sen-* signals old age.
related: Diachronic — change over time, of which aging is one kind

words.title: Surfeit
words.definition: An excessive amount of something; to cause someone to desire no more.
words.etymology: From Old French **surfaire** (to overdo), from *sur-* (over) + *faire* (to do), from Latin *superfacere*.
words.example: I am **surfeited** with shopping — one more store and I'll crack.
words.memoryHook: *Sur-* (over) + *faire* (to do) → to **surfeit** is to do or consume past the point of want.

words.title: Timorous
words.definition: Showing or suffering from nervousness, fear, or a lack of confidence.
words.etymology: From Old French **temoreus**, from Medieval Latin *timorosus*, from Latin *timor* (fear), from *timere* (to fear).
words.example: He asked the question in a **timorous** voice, expecting the answer he feared.
words.memoryHook: *Timor* is Latin for fear → **timorous** = full of fear. Think "timid."
related: minacious — the threatening flip side of fearful

words.title: Turpitude
words.definition: Depravity; wickedness.
words.etymology: From Latin **turpitudo** (baseness), from *turpis* (vile, base).
words.example: The nominee was rejected over acts of moral **turpitude** from his past.
words.memoryHook: *Turpis* = base/vile in Latin → **turpitude** = baseness. Think "moral turpitude."
related: Perfidious — a treacherous form of wickedness

words.title: Veracious
words.definition: Speaking or representing the truth; truthful.
words.etymology: From Latin **verax** (truthful), from *verus* (true).
words.example: The memoir was praised as a **veracious** account of the war, down to the smallest detail.
words.memoryHook: *Verus* = true in Latin → **veracious** = truthful. Compare its sibling **verity**.
related: verity — the noun form of the same root

words.title: Verity
words.definition: The quality of being true; a universally accepted truth.
words.etymology: From Latin **veritas** (truth), from *verus* (true).
words.example: Some **verities** — that power corrupts, that time wounds all heels — never lose their force.
words.memoryHook: *Verus* = true → **verity** = truth. Compare its adjective sibling **veracious**.
related: Veracious — the adjective from the same root

words.title: Welter
words.definition: To move in a turbulent fashion; a confused mass or state of disorder.
words.etymology: From Middle English **welteren**, from Middle Dutch / Low German *welteren* (to roll, tumble).
words.example: The attack petered out in a **welter** of bloody, confused fighting.
words.memoryHook: To **welter** is to wallow and roll — chaos that thrashes around.
related: imbroglio — another word for a confused tangle

words.title: Zugunruhe
words.definition: Restlessness at the beginning of a migration period.
words.etymology: From German **Zugunruhe**: *Zug* (migration) + *Unruhe* (restlessness). First documented use: 1950.
words.example: Captive birds start to pace and flutter with **zugunruhe** weeks before their wild kin leave.
words.memoryHook: *Zug* = "train" moving, *Unruhe* = unease → the animal's restless itch to get moving.
related: mimetic — another word about inherited behavior
